analysis.one_liner: Toughens EPA limits on ethylene oxide, a cancer-causing industrial gas, and requires public notice of violations.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote; it was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in May 2021 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Ethylene oxide is a gas used to sterilize medical equipment and make other chemicals, and EPA's own cancer review found it far more dangerous than older rules assumed. This bill would have ordered EPA to rewrite its emission standards for ethylene oxide based on that 2016 cancer assessment, apply the strictest available control technology to chamber exhaust vents at both large and small sources, run a new residual risk assessment, and tell the public within 30 days whenever a facility violated the standards — with an inspector general investigation if EPA stayed silent.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or attend school near facilities that emit ethylene oxide, including communities in Illinois and elsewhere where sterilization plants operate. EPA's 2016 assessment found the gas poses a much higher cancer risk than earlier rules assumed, so tighter emission limits and mandatory public notice of violations would directly lower their exposure and give them information they currently may not get.

how_it_helps.text: Orders EPA to rewrite its ethylene oxide emission standards based on the agency's 2016 finding that the gas is far more carcinogenic than assumed when the old rules were written.
Applies maximum achievable control technology requirements to chamber exhaust vents and extends the rules to both major and area sources of ethylene oxide.
Requires EPA to notify the public of any violation of the revised standards within 30 days, and triggers an Inspector General investigation into the health risks if EPA fails to do so.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that sterilize medical devices and other products with ethylene oxide, and chemical manufacturers that produce the gas, would bear the cost of new emission controls and monitoring. Some of those costs could be passed to hospitals and consumers through higher sterilization prices, and the bill sets a fast 180-day deadline for the revised standards.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ethylene oxide sterilization plants and producers

drawbacks.text: The 180-day deadline for EPA to finalize revised standards is unusually fast for a federal rulemaking that normally takes years of notice, comment, and technical review, which could produce a rushed or legally vulnerable rule.

Sterilization with ethylene oxide is how most disposable medical devices are made safe; tighter emission limits could raise sterilization costs for hospitals and medical suppliers, and a handful of plants handle much of the national volume, so severe compliance burdens could disrupt supply chains.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and specific: EPA's own 2016 cancer assessment concluded ethylene oxide is far more dangerous than the old standards assumed, and people living near emitting plants carry real cancer risk. The costs fall on a small number of sterilization and chemical facilities, and modern emission controls exist that can capture most of the gas. The main design flaw is the very short rulemaking deadline, but that does not offset the public health gain.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2021 and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin, joined by Senator Duckworth, introduced the bill on May 27, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No further action was taken: the committee never held a markup or vote, and the full Senate never considered the bill before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that emit ethylene oxide — medical-device sterilization plants and chemical producers — came out ahead, because they avoided stricter emission controls and mandatory public notice of violations, while residents near those plants got no relief from cancer-risk exposure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ethylene oxide emitters avoided new controls

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing EPA to revise ethylene oxide emission standards and require public notice of violations.

for.name: Sen. Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Joined as cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to; chaired by Sen. Tom Carper (D-DE) during the 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup, hearing action, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators supported the bill — both Illinois Democrats — and it never advanced far enough for a vote that would show how the parties lined up.

industries.industry: Medical-device and product sterilization companies (ethylene oxide emitters)
industries.note: These contract sterilization plants are the largest emitters of ethylene oxide, a potent carcinogen, often near residential neighborhoods. The bill would have forced them to install stricter emission controls and publicly disclose violations, so their interest in blocking it ran against nearby residents' health.

Producers of the gas are also covered sources under the Clean Air Act rules the bill targets and would face tighter limits on major and area sources. Their exposure liability would have grown if EPA had to adopt its 2016 cancer findings into enforceable standards.

They rely on ethylene oxide sterilization for disposable medical devices, so tighter rules could raise costs, but their patients' communities benefit from reduced emissions. The effect here is indirect and secondary.
